translations.text: The history of the life of Saint Peter the Iberian, bishop, distinguished confessor, and ascetic of our Lord.
We are commanded by Paul, the divine apostle, to remember our leaders, when he says:
“Remember your leaders, those who spoke the word of God to you. As you consider the outcome of their way of life, imitate their faith.”
Thus, as people paying a rightful debt that is pleasing to God, and fulfilling an apostolic command,
we are urged to do this diligently. For truly, a great road to salvation for disciples
who are zealous for good things and eager to imitate is the virtuous way of life of those who became leaders in God. But for us, it is not only a leader
but also a good shepherd, a loving father, a holy bishop, a confessor of devotion to God, and a martyr many times over
whose remembrance lies before us. He is equally beloved by everyone, by the speaker and the listeners alike.
Therefore, it is fitting that we speak and listen about him with complete eagerness, trusting in his holy prayers. Even if we cannot do so as he deserves, nevertheless,
with goodwill let us pay whatever part of our debt we can. We begin the history about him with the origins of his family line.
For it has fittingly been said, “God is among the generation of the righteous,” and “The generation of the righteous will be blessed,” and “A chosen people and a priestly kingdom.”
The homeland of the blessed Peter was the land of the Iberians, the renowned land of those northern peoples who live toward the east.
It is constantly contested by the Romans and the Persians, each of whom strives to make the country its own ally, through friendship, to obtain its assistance.
In the language of their country, his original name was Nabarnugius.
But when he was found worthy of the holy monastic habit, his name was then changed to Peter, after the chief of the apostles.
Perhaps, as I believe, the fathers who gave him the holy habit were moved by divine inspiration,

because he was destined to emulate him in his way of life, his character, and the boldness of his faith, which had been entrusted to him by God himself. It was because of this faith that our Lord named him Peter, that is, Rock,
and founded the orthodox church upon this rock, saying to him: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church,
and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it. I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be
loosed in heaven.” Now the father of the blessed Peter, our father and bishop, was Bosmarius, king of the Iberians.
His father’s father was also Bosmarius. His mother was Bacurduchtia, and his mother’s mother was the holy Duchtia. His maternal grandfather was the great Bacurius, Duchtia’s husband.
He was the first of those who ruled in that country to become a Christian king, and he guided that entire people to the worship of God.
All these, though they were kings and queens of the Iberians, also acquired the kingdom of heaven through their virtue.
His paternal grandmother was Osduchtia, the wife of Bosmarius and the mother of his father Bosmarius.
Pharasmanius was the brother of Osduchtia, his paternal grandmother. While he held an honored position at the court of Arcadius, emperor of the Romans,

He held the rank of a great general and occupied leading offices. Finally, when he fled from the plotting of Eudoxia, the wife of Arcadius, and managed to hide himself, he quickly reached his own country.
When he became king over the Iberians, he took the White Huns, who are neighbors of the Iberians, along with him and became the cause of many misfortunes for those subject to the Romans.
Now the great Bacurius, the maternal grandfather of the blessed Peter, had a holy brother, Arsilius.
He grew old alongside Bacurius and Bosmarius, already from the time of [?] rule over the Iberians,
and ended his life in virginity and complete holiness. The blessed Peter had no full brothers or sisters, but only a sister on his father's side, born of a concubine, whose name was Bomirusparia.
By his father's wish, she was regarded as his full sister. A holy and distinguished woman named Zuzu raised Peter while he was still a child.
He was kept hidden with her so that he would not be handed over as a hostage to the Persians, for he had sent envoys many times for this purpose.
This woman's daughter, who was called Ota, was the blessed man's nurse. She had also breastfed him when he was an infant.
Her husband was Curanius, and her full brother was Bardalius.
Their sons, Cata and Morgacis, were brought up with the blessed man and were his age.
Let no one, out of narrow-mindedness, consider this recounting of names unnecessary verbiage. We have not mentioned these people without a purpose.
Rather, that father, who cherished love and truly loved God, gathered all these names together
and celebrated their commemoration on one day each year, on the Saturday of the middle week of Lent.
He offered them this repayment for the peace they had provided him, which he had chosen for himself so that he might renounce the world.
For this reason, we too, insignificant as we are, thought it right not to deprive of remembrance those whom he considered worthy of commemoration and from whom such a flower had sprung.
For there certainly are lovers of virtue who will gain great benefits when they hear the account of these people. Now the great Bacurius,
who was the first of the kings of the Iberians to become a Christian, and Dukhtia, his wife, reached such a height of reverence for God
and of virtue and conduct in Christ that, although they were monarchs, they practiced asceticism and lived a monastic life while reigning.
For the two of them, having reached a good agreement by mutual consent, abstained from sexual relations, since the children they had been granted were enough for them.
The faithful Bacurius devoted himself to fasting, prayer, and almsgiving, and three times a week he swept the city's church with his own hands.
Since his love for the poor was exceedingly abundant, he considered it no trouble to prepare various dishes in his palace.
He carried these in baskets and personally took them at night to the poorhouse he had built. The king himself fed those who lay there with his own hands.
The blessed Dukhtia, his wife and companion in zeal, cast aside all her royal finery and clothed herself in sackcloth.
She sold all the gold and pearls from her litter, which is called a basternion, and distributed the proceeds to the poor.
She often continued fasting and praying for weeks, and she received such grace from our Lord that she could bring about healing simply by laying on her hands.
Now concerning the great Bacurius, who was this woman’s husband.

It is fitting that we should not pass over this account. For, along with his other virtues, he once won the crown of confession of the faith—or rather, in his intention, the crown of martyrdom as well.
For once, when he was going to war with the king of the Persians, as someone who had established a treaty of peace with him,
and as his military commander, he saw that, as soon as the sun rose, the king himself and all the commanders and consuls
and satraps and all the nobles suddenly leaped down from their horses and worshiped the sun. He himself remained seated on his horse.
When the other satraps reported this to the king, Bacurius stood before him
and was asked whether what had been reported about him was true. With boldness he cried out before the entire army—
a man who truly shared the zeal of Daniel and the three young men, his companions—“I am a Christian, and I am not permitted
to abandon him who alone is the true God and Creator of everything and worship his creation, which was created to give light in service to me and to all humanity.”
The king was so astonished and so cowed by his boldness that he turned and said privately to his own men, “He is Bacurius, and we need him.
What can we do to him?” These are some of Bacurius’s victories. Now Arsilius was this man’s own brother,
the one whom we mentioned above, who governed the kingdom of the Iberians in old age and virginity, together with Bosmarius, the father
of our Peter, who was also called Nabarnugius. When the leading men of the country repeatedly urged and begged him
to marry in order to produce children and continue the royal line, and brought him a woman of royal descent, he remained a virgin while living with her.
But when he learned that she had done something shameful, she denied it when he gently reproached her. Finally, however, he unexpectedly caught that wicked man.
Oh, the humility and great gentleness of his philosophical way of life! He said to him, “Look, your life and your blood are spared.
Here are provisions and money for your journey. Leave quickly, and do not remain in this country, lest you meet a terrible death and your blood be charged against me.”
After letting him go in this way, he then said to his wife, “Because you have done this, I will not divorce you, nor will I expose your shame to ridicule.
But I trust in the Son of God, whose law you have violated, that he will cause your private parts [?] to swarm with worms, and that your flesh will perish in this way.”
Immediately the curse of that chaste man took effect. The area beneath her belly rotted with worms, and her life and flesh were wasting away in bitter suffering.
All this continued until she went about as nothing but dry bones and skin. Yet the zeal of that righteous man also brought deliverance out of the curse.
For as she was being chastened by the divine blow, she came to recognize her transgression and was filled with deep remorse. She groaned bitterly.
She turned to confession and came to such repentance and contrition of heart that she would publicly throw herself down before the church door and reveal her sin before everyone.
She begged everyone to trample on her, calling herself a disgraceful prostitute, an adulteress, an enemy of God, and a reproach to humanity.
Through this she moved everyone to compassion, tears, and shared suffering.
And when all the people fasted together, and the church earnestly offered supplication on her behalf, with perseverance, tears, and groans, she was healed of her affliction.
After these things she became holy through virtuous conduct and ascetic discipline, so that she might be an example and a demonstration to everyone of the way of grace and salvation.
This faithful Arsilius, through his virtuous conduct, found such favor and confidence before God that he performed miracles through his prayers,
as our blessed father himself firmly and truthfully testified.
While he was reigning over the Iberians, he learned that blessed Peter had withdrawn from the world and was living in the Holy City,
and that he was practicing the disciplines of monastic life there, as the narrative will show as it proceeds with God's help. He sent him a letter, saying, “Because it is written:
'Blessed is the man who has offspring in Zion and members of his household in Jerusalem,' as we have you, I beg you, my son, to pray for me, so that through
your prayers I may find mercy.” And because many rulers of the earth, who love pleasures and are believers, customarily provide themselves with male and female singers—
these empty things of the world, who sing for amusement and corrupting pleasure—he appointed singers of sacred songs for himself, like King David,
who sang the holy words of God in the evenings and at all times, so that his palace would be no different from a church.
Now Osdukhtia, blessed Peter's paternal grandmother, was so holy that after her death, when a certain guardhouse was being built
and kept collapsing because of an earthquake, they brought her body and laid it there as that of one of the saints, and immediately it stopped collapsing.
Blessed Zuzu, who brought up the blessed man, was so holy that, when he was a child
and slept beside her, she would often drench him with tears as she stood at night and said these words in the Iberian language:
“My Lord Jesus, my God and the giver of my life, have mercy on me.” Once, when an earthquake occurred and shook everything, this blessed woman ran around her house,
which had eight apses, and grasped each of the pillars, crying out confidently, “Lord, see how I have served you! Have pity on me and on my children!”
Her supplication did not allow her house to suffer any loss, although that earthquake brought ruin upon many at that time. There was
also in that city a certain prominent man who was greedy and wronged many people.
Although she rebuked him many times, he would not give up his greed.
But when she prayed, fire suddenly came down from heaven and consumed all his fields, which were already nearly ready for harvest.
This woman's daughter, who was called Ota and who also brought up the blessed man, spent all her days in holiness, fasting, and prayer.
Now Bakurdukhtia, the mother of our holy father, remained a widow after her husband's death.
She would not consent to marry a second husband, but persevered in fasting and prayer. She no longer agreed to live in the city,
but wished to live a monastic life on her estates, and built guesthouses for strangers and hospitals everywhere.
When the blessed man heard that she was going to come and visit him, he fled to Cyprus so that he would not see her face.
When she learned this, she no longer came. Nor had he ever been willing, from the time he took the monastic habit, to write to any of his own people,
or to receive letters from anyone. He himself told us this many times.
From such a holy root and from such holy parents sprang a rose blossom: the blessed Saint Peter.
He was brought up by such God-fearing guardians, fittingly and in keeping with the character of those who had given him birth and raised him.
He became a chosen vessel, as it is written, honored, sanctified, useful to his master, and prepared for every good work, to bear the name of Christ
and to praise and proclaim the orthodox faith before all people, and, from his childhood until his last breath, to remain steadfast as a disciple
of the apostles and a faithful imitator of them, always carrying the cross of Christ and filled with the Holy Spirit.
Through his grace and power, he won many over to obedience to Christ and the gospel.
He offered himself as an example of every good thing and of virtuous conduct, according to the apostolic exhortation: in speech, in conduct,
in love, in faith, in purity, and as a glorious pillar of the orthodox faith.
Through his holy prayers he became a wall of protection for the whole world, like Noah of old, while the ark was being tossed about in the latter flood of chastisement.
But his manifold virtues in God and his conduct according to the gospel, which were outstandingly evident at every stage of his life
and grew with him through divine grace—it is beyond the weakness and poverty of our words to undertake to write of them at length and bring the account to [?].
For I fear that, as I venture into the boundless and unfathomable deep of his achievements,
having neither the experience nor the ability to swim, I may be overwhelmed and drowned by the surging waves of the grace that accompanied him,
and that, because of my lowliness and weakness, his virtue may suffer loss.
Therefore, each of his deeds and gifts, which at different times, in different ways, and in different circumstances
were manifested through the grace of God: in ascetic discipline and abstinence, and, to speak in the apostle’s words, in hardships,
in necessities, in afflictions, in persecutions, in labors, in fasts, in vigils, in conflicts, in battles,
in struggles to the point of bloodshed—not against sin alone, nor against flesh and blood, but against rulers and authorities,
against the world rulers of this darkness, against the spirits of wickedness; with great endurance,
with the power of signs, wonders, and healings, with the power of the Holy Spirit, through the weapons of righteousness
on the right and on the left, through glory and dishonor, through abuse and praise. For he was as one unknown, and yet he was known.
To his God alone he was known as fully as he ought to be known. He was as one dead to the flesh, yet he was always alive and fervent in spirit.
He was as one poor, yet he enriched many, nourishing both souls and bodies with the food appropriate to each.
As one who had nothing yet possessed everything—not only on earth, but also in the treasuries in heaven.
For he had treasures stored up there, where his heart, his thoughts, and his way of life always were. These things, and everything that accompanied them,
were nobly accomplished by him through the grace of Christ who dwelt in him, to inspire zeal in many and bring them salvation.
Since I cannot describe them accurately and reliably and set them down as a history, I leave them aside and refer those who love such things
to the mouths of all those who have long been holy, who have heard these things many times.
I advise one to learn these things, which are as though written in sacred books, and to become filled with the knowledge and benefit they provide. For they are renowned everywhere,
and even without anyone asking, they are proclaimed by divine grace itself. Let no one disbelieve what is being told,
but rather let the hearer consider that it falls short of the truth. For what time or speech would suffice to recount
accurately the things that the grace of Christ accomplished through his hands and with him—for the salvation, as I have said, and encouragement of those who wish to strive zealously in good deeds,
and, for many, for the establishment, building up, and strengthening of the orthodox faith and of his catholic Church,
of which he appointed him chief priest and shepherd? And in what manner? Let no one, like those who delight in finding fault, say, “He took and seized such an honor for himself.”
Rather, he was called by grace from above with a divine calling worthy of wonder, which I cannot pass over even though I am in a hurry.
Instead, I will explain it as fully as I can in a few words, taking the account back a little to its beginning.
For, like the patriarch Isaac, he too was conceived and born through a promise. We will briefly recount how this happened at the appropriate time.
When his father Bosmarius was returning from a country estate to the city, he reached a torrent along the way. It was flowing strongly and blocking passage along the road.
Forced to stop on its bank, he was deep in thought when he saw someone who said to him, “Bosmarius, look, the river is now passable for you.
Get up, cross over, and go into your house. Have intercourse with your wife, and she will conceive and bear you a son who will be honored before God and before people.”
Thus, after he had been conceived, born, and brought up through such divine grace, while he was still twelve years old, he was sent as a hostage
to the God-fearing Christian Theodosius the Younger, emperor of the Romans.
After the emperor had repeatedly requested this, sending envoys, he was sent by his father Bosmarius, who at that time ruled the land of the Iberians.
He preferred friendship with the Romans, as Christians, to the assistance of the impious Persians.
He was sent with great pomp and honor. When he came to the blessed Theodosius, he was affectionately received by him
and was brought up and loved by him like a son. He saw the emperor’s devotion to the fear of God and the love of Christ,
and that of Empress Eudoxia, his wife and companion in zeal, and of the men and women who served them,
and especially of the eunuchs called chamberlains. For all of them lived in the palace as though in a monastery.
Through prayers, fasts, services at night, and the other things that please God, he was set ablaze with zeal.
And since he had inherited from his parents a love of God like a spark of fire,
he diligently nurtured it day by day through spiritual progress and ascetic discipline, until he filled his soul with a great, blazing flame of heavenly grace.
Underneath, against his body, he wore a garment of hair. On the outside, however, he wrapped himself in a splendid, luxurious garment to conceal his virtue.
His food was what Daniel and his companions had eaten, and even this in a small quantity, once every three days
or four days. Sometimes he took it only once a week, to subdue the flesh, which loves correction,
and its unruly impulses. The ground was the bed of this young and tender prince.
While he conducted himself in this way, cleansing himself from every defilement of flesh and spirit and growing in stature, he became a temple of God, filled with the Holy Spirit.
All this went so far that, through divine grace, while he was still a boy, many healings, signs, and great miracles were accomplished through his hands, even within the palace itself.
So that I do not weary my listeners altogether, I will leave aside the other things and first set down one of them, sufficient to confirm them all.
For he possessed the bones of holy martyrs who were Persian by birth and who had indeed suffered martyrdom in those times.
Following the tradition and practice of the blessed man, we still name their names, celebrate their commemorations, and read the accounts of their martyrdoms.
He had placed these with honor in a small shrine [?], in the very chamber where he practiced his ascetic discipline. There he slept on the ground before them.
He performed the divine services with lights, incense, hymns, and petitions. As he offered them every honor and comfort, he would see
them plainly on many occasions, singing psalms with him, keeping vigil with him, and praying with him.
Once, then, as the holy feast of Epiphany approached, when custom requires all the senators
to see the king and to be seen by one another, he shut himself in the martyrs’ chamber and with his own hands carried out all the decoration of that house of prayer.
He wiped the walls and ceiling, and swept and washed the floor. Then, after washing and polishing many lamps, he hung them on a [?].
He sent to his steward and ordered that oil be brought to him to keep the lights burning.
But the steward was distressed because he paid no attention to worldly affairs, and was eager for him to be seen like the other nobles.
Moreover, being influenced by the devil himself, he became angry and said, “Great are the hopes concerning this fellow, his country, and ourselves! Though he was sent by them
to the Romans for royal honor and glory, he wants to become a monk and make all of us who accompany him miserable.”
And he refused to send oil. But the holy young man and philosopher, perceiving the enemy’s activity,
displayed strict observance of the gospel through peacefulness and patience at such an age. Instead of anger, he turned to prayer.
And, fervent in faith and spirit, he called upon the prayers of these saints. When the evening of the vigil arrived, with water
He simply prepared and lit all the lamps without oil. Throughout these seven days of the holy feast, they continued burning without interruption, night and day.
When this was heard by the emperor, all his household, and the senate, it brought them all to amazement.
Thus many came to desire to emulate his way of life and his ascetic discipline.
A considerable number of such people gathered around him, practicing ascetic discipline with him and matching his zeal. Therefore, on one of those days,
while he was standing among them and speaking with them about matters concerning their salvation, he suddenly saw our Lord among them in the appearance of a monk.
He fell down, worshiped him, and clasped his feet, though no one saw him except he alone.
He cried out with weeping and tears, saying, “My Lord and my God!” He thought that the others also saw him.
But they did not see him; he alone saw him. Thus all those around him were filled with great amazement, fear, and trembling,
so that, when they learned of the divine vision that had appeared to him, they might increase their divine zeal and love still further.
Because of this, many of them also renounced the world and took the monastic habit after he himself became a monk.
He even used to tell us their names. Among them were the God-bearing monk Theodotus and his brothers,
Proclus and Sophronius, distinguished in authority. They were also sons [?]
and administrators of the imperial estate. But these are only a very few of the many gifts of the blessed man while he was young and living in the palace, which we have recounted in passing.
As he advanced in stature and in divine love, he set ascents in his heart, according to the saying of David, who sings sacred songs,
and passed from one light to another, higher and more revealed. He longed to withdraw from the world and its vanity and to run toward the first of the virtues,
which is living as a stranger. Although he tried many times to escape, he could not, for the devil and the demons became aware of it.
And the members of his household—I mean his servants, those spear-bearers who escorted him—
became so enraged, out of their hatred for him, that they tried many times to kill him secretly.
Had the Lord’s protection alone not prevented it, they would have carried out their reckless deed.
Nor was this all: the God-fearing emperor Theodosius was also concerned to keep him as a hostage, lest, when that people demanded him back,
and he failed to present him as he had received him, he should turn them into enemies and opponents instead of friends and allies. So he summoned him,
and threatened him about this, keeping him under close guard so that he would not escape secretly. But there is nothing

stronger than the power of Christ, nor anything more ardent than the love of those who love him purely. He who had loved him from childhood as he had Samuel, and had shepherded him as he had Israel and Joseph,
was guiding and guarding him like a sheep. It was he who fulfilled his good desire for the monastic habit, with a mighty hand and an uplifted arm,
through signs and wonders, just as he had once snatched Israel from the tyranny of the Egyptians and brought them into the promised land, flowing with milk and honey.
He appointed the holy martyrs as helpers in his escape, guides, guardians, and companions. They had been well cared for by him.
For the more his love of fleeing from the world set him aflame, the more the demons and their human helpers hindered him in this, vigilantly and carefully watching
his coming and going, his wishes and his thoughts. And when he found the man who had been given to him by God, the blessed John—Marginal note: the eunuch—
a man of the same disposition and zeal as himself, who shared his longing for eternal life and was a helper on the road leading to it,
who came originally from the region of Laodicea and was adorned with every kind of reverence for God, gentleness, and chastity,
and faith and humility, he took this man with him, bound him to himself with the bond of love, and made him his companion, like Paul
with Barnabas. He relied on him as an adviser and companion in the flight to salvation. And because he knew that it was through the activity of demons that their thoughts were not kept hidden,
but became known and were disclosed by them, he took John to the little garden where the bones of the holy martyrs were laid.
Both of them put their heads over these bones and spoke with one another there. In this way they made an agreement about the time and manner of their escape.
From then on no one knew or disclosed anything, neither demons nor human beings, until the plan was carried out. The holy martyrs themselves
took them away at an unusual hour of the night, through such watch posts in the imperial city, despite all this and other such obstacles.
They also filled their hearts with great courage and strength. For they used to see them, as I often heard the blessed man himself recount to those who loved him,
who could also benefit from such accounts, going ahead of them in the darkness like a cloud or a pillar of fire, and guiding them.
And, wonder of wonders, they were praising and singing together in harmony, with a tuneful and sweet voice, this divine hymn,
whose very words I also set down. They are these: “Seek Christ, and see the light from light and the incomprehensible glory.
He rewards those who seek him.” The blessed man also remembered the melody of the hymn.
They did not stop singing aloud in this way as the holy martyrs themselves went ahead of them and guided them, until they reached the harbor.
When they knew that they were now safe, they confidently looked for a boat. Once again, through the help and assistance of the martyrs, they found one and immediately crossed over.
But they were afraid that they might be caught if they were pursued or recognized at the place called Stena—
for the gates and harbors of the city were guarded for three days after their departure, with the aim of finding them—so they put on different clothing, poor and suitable for slaves.
Through the protection of God, who went with them and guided them, they managed to remain unrecognized by those stationed at Stena who were making inquiries about them.
From there they left the boat and traveled on foot. The two of them made their journey through the region of Epirus alone,
with the holy martyrs, who were their guardians and companions.
They carried their precious bones in a small gold chest, just as the great Moses carried the ark of God with the cherubim.
They also carried only a small book of John the Evangelist, in which a piece of wood from the holy, precious, and saving cross had been fixed.
by which they were being protected. Our Lord displayed many signs and no small number of miracles through it, giving it a gentle power to strengthen and comfort them. It remained
for the whole week of the journey, that fragment of the cross, pouring out oil abundantly.
And all this was so that they could receive it in their hands and anoint their faces and bodies, while the oil continued to flow still more abundantly.
This, indeed, is what the prophet calls the oil of gladness: the grace and power of the Holy Spirit,
which was rejoicing and exulting together with the power of the cross—that cross which those holy men had gone out to take up, and to follow gladly the God who was crucified.
It increased their gladness still further and sustained it through wonders like these. It also made their arrival known through the holy martyrs.
For as they traveled along the road and passed through regions, cities, and villages, although they were entirely unknown
to the inhabitants of those regions and to those traveling with them, in most places they would find, outside the gates and entrances,
crowds of children, men, and women with branches and lamps, as though they had come out to meet the martyrs, sitting outside the walls.
They would ask those coming in where they were and who they were—the people carrying the bones of the holy martyrs.
For they said, “Yesterday some of them arrived, announcing the news and instructing us to go out to meet them.”
Thus, greatly amazed at our Lord’s care for them, and with increased gladness and firmness of heart, they traveled easily and without hardship, with courage
and joy, as people sheltered by such a hand.
Now a man belonging to those called bar-adre [?], who was known for his authority, overtook them on the road and supposed that they were runaway slaves.
Hoping to take them into his own service and slavery, he unsettled them with intimidation and threats and ordered them to go with him. So they followed him.
For what could they do, being led away like foreign slaves and captives, except lift their eyes upward to the Lord
and cry out in their hearts and call upon their protectors, the holy martyrs? That very night, the martyrs came upon the man with many rebukes,
threatening complete destruction for him and his entire household unless he released the young men in peace,
as men of God who took refuge in him and hastened to him. They instructed him to release them with honor.
Indeed, filled with fear and trembling, he rose early in the morning at once, fell on his face before them, and sought relief from them.
He earnestly urged them to remain in his region, promising to build them a monastery, assign it sufficient income, and provide them with every comfort.
For he was a wealthy man in that region. When they would not agree, he released them with great honors and comforts, treating them as masters and helpers—
the man who had previously hoped to become their master. Thus they were released with honor and in a wonderful manner,
and their affection and love for our Lord, and their faith in the holy martyrs, grew still greater. Throughout the entire journey and in every place,
they enjoyed such care, protection, and guidance from God that the words of Moses applied to them: “Like an eagle sheltering its nest.”
And he cherishes his young, spreads his wings and receives them, and carries them on his strong pinions. The Lord alone led them.
There was no foreign god with them. He surrounded them, guided them, and guarded them like the pupil of an eye. He supplied their needs along the way.
He brought them up and settled them on the heights of the holy land. Rejoicing and celebrating together, they made the journey from New Rome to Jerusalem as though it were only a short distance.
They continually moved from one lodging to another, and from strangers to strangers, while the love that burned within them
continually stole away and soothed the weakness caused by traveling along the road.
When they drew near Jerusalem, the holy city they loved, they looked from the height opposite it, about five stadia away,
and saw the lofty roofs of the holy and revered churches gleaming like the rising sun: the church of the saving and revered Cross, and that of the holy Resurrection,
and also that of the revered Ascension on the mountain opposite the city. They cried out loudly, fulfilling that prophetic saying: “Look upon Zion,
the city of our salvation! Let your eyes see Jerusalem!” And with all their strength they offered glory and thanksgiving to Christ, whom they loved,
to him who had called them, brought them out, guided them, and rescued them. Throwing themselves facedown, they did not cease bowing in worship from the top of that height,
crawling on their knees and repeatedly greeting that holy land with their lips and their eyes,
in the fullness of the love that blazed within them, until they were inside the holy walls.
They embraced the very base of the precious Cross—I mean holy Golgotha—and the place of the holy Resurrection.
Together they gazed and wept, gave thanks and praise, and rejoiced, as though they had already received Jesus, whom they loved, and were now dwelling with him in heaven.
To cut the account short, leaving much untold: God, who had guarded and rescued them,
since they were strangers and unfamiliar with these holy places, himself guided them to good hosts,
and to teachers and helpers in their holy desire. He had prepared a good hostess for them beforehand: I mean the blessed Melania, the Roman woman.
She, together with her husband Pinianus and her mother Albina, belonged to those who held the foremost rank in the Roman senate, in ancestry, wealth, and prestige,
and in all the splendor of these other things. They were even related to the imperial family. But they loved Christ with a true love, and above everything else they
honored him. They laid up for themselves wealth that stands firm and endures forever, in place of wealth that passes away, slips away, perishes, and brings destruction.
They despised all these things and followed him, having completely stripped themselves of the world. The greater part of their possessions,
those that could readily be disposed of, they distributed to the poor and needy throughout the Roman Empire, and also to holy churches and monasteries.
They abandoned all the rest and counted it as dung. Lovingly girding themselves with the cross of our Lord, they came to the holy city to worship him.
When they arrived there and came to love living there, they established two large monasteries, with many inhabitants, on the holy Mount of Olives,
beside the place of the holy Ascension: one for men and the other for women. They endowed both with an income.
For the praise and glory of God, and for the welcome and salvation of the many souls who came there for their salvation.
While they lived quietly in these places, in complete ascetic discipline, stillness, abstinence, and humility, they fought the good fight.
They embraced poverty even in their clothing, for their clothing was made of rough haircloth—humble and lowly clothing.
Keeping faithfully to the yoke of crucifixion with Christ, they provided each day, through the work of their hands, the nourishment their weak bodies needed.
Pinianus carried wood on his shoulders from far away in the wilderness and sold it in the marketplace without grumbling. The blessed woman, meanwhile,
worked at preparing wool. From this she supplied her modest needs for nourishment and distributed what remained to the needy.
So when she heard of the arrival in Jerusalem of Peter and John, the holy young men—
at that time they were called Nabarnugius and Mithradates in the languages of their homelands—and learned who they were and where they came from, she welcomed them joyfully.
For she remembered that when she had once come to Constantine’s imperial city, she had seen the blessed Peter there, while he was still a boy being brought up like a prince.
She had loved him greatly, because she saw that the grace of Christ had rested upon him from his youth. For, as I have said, he had been dear to God from his infancy.
The reason for the blessed Melania’s coming to the imperial city was this.
When one of the distinguished men of Rome came to the God-fearing Emperor Theodosius, having been sent by Emperor Valentinian
to arrange the betrothal of the blessed Theodosius’s daughter to him, this man was a relative of Saint Melania.
He did not yet share in the grace of the Christians, but he longed to see the blessed Melania and promised to become a Christian
if he could meet her and hear from her the word of salvation. As I have said, the Christ-loving emperor sent for the blessed woman and urged her to come as far as the city
of the emperor, for the salvation of a soul. She came and, through the divine grace that dwelt in her, made him a believer and a fully committed Christian.
She also built up many others and guided them toward a godly way of life like her own, and she stirred the blessed Peter’s desire still more to emulate her zeal.
Then she returned to the holy city, maintaining her former way of life and ascetic discipline.
Since there was also another Melania in Jerusalem, from among the distinguished Romans,
who had likewise renounced the world and taken the monastic habit, it should be understood that the other was the elder, while this one, who welcomed the holy men, was the younger.
Before these two there had been another woman, distinguished by her family and wealth, very chaste and God-fearing,
whose name was Poemenia. She loved to live in the holy and revered places. It was her way of life
and her love that these women who have been mentioned sought to emulate. She also built the Church of the Holy Ascension and surrounded it with buildings.
She also overthrew the idol on the mountain called Gerizim in Samaria, which was still standing and had been worshiped by the inhabitants of that region up to that time.
It was therefore this younger Melania, the wife of Pinianus and daughter of Albina, who joyfully welcomed those holy men as beloved sons.
For when they were received by her there [?], they were honored in that monastery for men for their exemplary ascetic conduct. Together they were also found worthy of the monastic habit
at holy hands, those of the holy and renowned Gerontius,
who was a priest and abbot of the holy Mount of Olives. For this Gerontius too, whose story is well known,
was a native of Jerusalem. While he was still a boy, he was taken into the protective care of Saint Melania and her husband.

When he had been brought up with them in holiness and in a way pleasing to God, they considered him worthy to share also in the sacred monastic habit, since his conduct and character were consistent with it.
The two of them took him alone and brought him to the holy tomb of our Savior. They placed the garments of the habit on the holy stone and clothed him as though from the hands of our Lord.
He asked that, together with the sacred clothing, these three things might be granted to him: right faith, holiness, and tears. And so he was found worthy of all three,
and especially of the gift of tears. Thus, when he was ordained priest and also appointed abbot on the holy Mount of Olives and over the monasteries there,
he would often celebrate three assemblies for divine worship on a single day of the week, especially on holy Sunday:
one on the holy mountain, one in that monastery for men, and another in that monastery for women. On the remaining days,
he celebrated an assembly and a private service every day for the blessed Melania, according to the custom of the Church of Rome. At each of these assemblies, when he began
the holy service, he would shed tears without stopping until the end, with pain and contrition of heart, so that none of those assembled could restrain themselves.
The whole congregation was filled with repentance, stirred to cries and sighs, and shed tears as he did.
Therefore, having rightly been found worthy of such grace, he also showed an end worthy of it.
For he lived to see the times of persecution brought by the lawless Council of Chalcedon, and during them he displayed the zeal of a martyr,
even enduring chains, imprisonment, and appearances before judges. He won the crown of confessing the faith, and so his life came to its end.
Although the authorities and many distinguished people urged him repeatedly merely to agree to speak with Juvenal the apostate, without entering into communion with him,
and so be released from his affliction, he would not consent at all. Instead, he said, “May the Lord forbid that I should see the face of Judas the betrayer!”
It was his hands that bestowed the habit on our fathers, Peter and John.
He himself changed their names to these names, in place of these names—in place of the names they had been given in their homelands.
There they now lived in stillness and exemplified ascetic virtue,
in that monastery for men, as I said before, where Gerontius himself was abbot.
There they also laid the honored bones of these holy martyrs, good guides and their companions, together with the bones of those forty martyrs,
the renowned martyrs of Sebaste. The holy and blessed Cyril, archbishop of Alexandria, officiated at the deposition of these relics.
For he had been persuaded by that faithful and orthodox empress, Eudocia,
that he should come for the deposition of the honored bones of Stephen, glorious and praised by all, the first of the martyrs and the chief of the deacons,
and dedicate the beautiful church that she had built outside the northern gates of the holy city, he gladly accepted the invitation.
When he came with a large number of bishops from throughout Egypt, he splendidly celebrated the deposition of the holy bones of the first martyr
on the fifteenth of the month of May. Then, immediately afterward, on the sixteenth of the same month,
at the urging of Saint Melania, he also celebrated the deposition of the holy Persian martyrs and of the forty martyrs with them on the Mount of Olives,
in the venerable church that had likewise been splendidly built by Empress Eudocia herself, as the inscription written there on the wall also makes known.
But let us return to the subject before us. When our common father had thus been found worthy of the holy habit,
having already passed twenty years of age, together with his fellow laborer John, he thereafter lived there in solitude,
and displayed conduct worthy of his habit, leading a life of abstinence and great ascetic discipline. The stubborn unruliness of the flesh, so prone to slipping, which stands opposed to
the spirit, and its rebellious will, which is hostile to God and cannot submit to the law of God—with hunger, thirst, sleeping on the ground, and keeping vigil,
and with these harsh practices he subdued and subjected them. He carried his ascetic discipline to this extent, until he checked the turbulence of youthful impulses
and extinguished the flame of the passions. Thus he enabled the spirit readily to find peace
and occupy itself with contemplation and gain mastery over the flesh—or rather, to bring both into a single harmony. Within dry skin and bones
he confined that great strength and bodily beauty, so that already he was bent over, bowed down by extreme emaciation and great ascetic discipline,
although formerly he had been very robust and strikingly distinguished by his large physique.
How many battles, how many struggles, and how many trials he endured, fighting ceaselessly against the Accuser and against his demons, the spirits of wickedness,
by night and by day—not only in dreams and apparitions, but, as the saying goes, hand to hand and face to face—
as he continually withdrew and went to the wilderness of John the Forerunner, who was the first leader and teacher of this kind of evangelical life.
I mean the wilderness that stretches toward the Jordan. There he practiced his way of life, communing alone with God alone and pursuing the struggle for virtue with greater
strictness and courage. What help and consolation he was granted by God, neither the weakness of our speech can record nor the available time allows.
Therefore, passing over many things, I think that the event especially worthy of remembrance and narration, which happened to him at the beginning,
when he received the habit, must be set down as an illustration of the things I have left out,
and for the benefit of those who hear. For when he saw the blessed Passarion, who greatly loved the poor and welcomed strangers,
who, besides his other godly virtues and acts of charity, had built a house for the poor outside the eastern gates of the city
for the rest and consolation of those whose bodies were sorely afflicted by infirmity, and had established a large and beautiful monastery within the walls of holy Zion,
He longed to imitate this good practice himself: the worship and singing of those who continually praise the Lord without ceasing.
He resolved to build a house with the Lord’s help and establish there a fixed number of holy monks who would praise the Lord. But before he began the work, he became weak, falling seriously ill.
While he lay gravely ill, he saw the devil standing before him, openly laughing at him, taunting him, and saying:
“Look! See what the one you love has done to you. See where the one you followed has brought you—the one for whose sake you left everything.
Now say something against him and get well.” But he blew at him and grew indignant,
and, as someone who had often experienced his insolence, said to him:
“Are you speaking about my Jesus, you filthy, insolent dog, you enemy of God and blasphemer? Are you advising me to do your work? May the power of Christ put an end to you!”
As soon as he heard the name of Christ, that evil one dissolved like smoke and disappeared.
Then Peter began to weep and call upon the Lord with bitter tears and sighs.
The Lord immediately appeared to him, in accordance with what is written, “While you are still speaking, I will say, ‘Here I am, close at hand,’” and said to him:

“What is wrong with you? Why are you disheartened, fainthearted one? Do you not know that I have authority over life and death, and that whether you live or die is in my hands? But if you are distressed about this,
because you have not been able to fulfill your vow and the pledge you made to build me a temple, as you previously desired, lift up your eyes and see.”

When he looked toward heaven, he saw a beautiful and glorious church, filled with light and glory. In it about fifty men were standing in an orderly line, clearly not in separate choirs, conducting worship and singing.
A voice came to him, saying, “Here is the church you promised to build me. Here too are those who sing. Do not be distressed any longer.” When he had said these things, the Lord departed from him.
He bowed down in worship and rejoiced, and was filled still more with strength, cheerfulness, and faith. Thus, having received assurance through this vision,
he arranged for the brothers who were with him to stand and sing in this way, organized in rows.
Through his prayers, this same order has endured and been preserved by his brothers to this day. But we must return to the rest of the narrative.
Keeping our account as brief as possible, let us take it up again where we left off.
For we remember that we promised, with God’s help, to explain how he moved away from Jerusalem
and came to live in the region of Gaza, the city beside the sea; how he was also deemed worthy of the priesthood, and finally of the office of bishop,
through the choice of divine grace. Jerusalem, the holy city, the city of the great King, in which the mystery of salvation for the whole world was accomplished
through the appearing of our God and Savior Christ, had long before been destroyed by the Romans, after the Jews’ outrageous acts against Christ,
in accordance with the predictions of all the prophets and Christ’s own sentence of judgment. Eventually it was rebuilt and settled again on a more extensive scale,
in the days of Constantine, the faithful, Christ-loving emperor, the father and patriarch of all Christian emperors, who was truly a chosen new David,
and by his God-fearing, blessed mother Helena, who equaled him in zeal and was truly his genuine mother.
For this God-loving queen, with fervent faith marked by reverence for God and with divine zeal
firmly established, and with her son as her helper and companion in zeal, did not hesitate to come in person to the holy places of Christ.
First, after searching for and finding, with divine help, the saving wood of the precious cross, she set it up for the whole world to venerate and for the healing of souls and bodies,
for whose sake he was also nailed to it. Afterward she erected for our Lord great buildings worthy of God, and splendid sanctuaries,
over our Lord’s divine tomb and at the holy place of the Skull, the venerated Golgotha, which is the true Holy of Holies and the true altar,
which was proclaimed and foreshadowed long ago in a mystery by the prophet Moses: composed by nature of stones neither cut nor worked.
For what other altar is like this, except this altar alone, which is truly Christ’s indivisible altar
and admits neither cutting nor division? On it the true Lamb of God was slaughtered and offered, he who takes away the sin of the world.
But since our account has brought us to this point, and we have mentioned the venerated cross, I think it fitting
that a certain mystery and a great and awe-inspiring miracle, which happened in the blessed man’s presence through its divine power, for the glory of God, for the full assurance of Christians’ hope,
and for the support and strengthening of our faith, should be set down in my account and brought before us. For the blessed man himself was a witness and eyewitness of it,
that son of the truth, our faithful father. He himself also recounted it many times and before many people, obeying the prophet who says:
“Make his mighty deeds known among the nations, recount all his wonders, and glory in his holy name. Remember these marvelous deeds that he has done.”
For while he was still a young man and was being brought up in the palace with the blessed Emperor Theodosius, he was able to obtain a fragment of the cross
from the clerics who customarily came from Jerusalem to honor the emperor and brought him blessings.
He kept this carefully and reverently, concealed in a little wax, which he wrapped in finely worked fabric.
He placed it in a gold casket, and every Sunday, especially on the appointed festivals, he would bring it out. After receiving a blessing from it and kissing it, he would put it back in its place.
Then one day, while he was doing this, after falling on his face, kissing it, and receiving a blessing, he called one of the chamberlains who were with him.
He regarded this man as more trustworthy and more intimate than the others, and at that moment the man happened to be alone with him. He urged him also to bow down and receive a blessing.
But when the man approached and came to place his face upon that holy fragment and receive a blessing,
while it was wrapped, as I said before, in wax and that worked fabric, it suddenly became a white dove. Flying from the holy man’s hands, it circled around the room,
flying and looking for a way out. When this happened, the blessed man was astonished and cried out.
Leaping up, he went around and ran through the room, trying to catch the dove.
But when it found a way out through a window, it disappeared from sight. That fragment, together with the wax and the worked fabric, was never seen again afterward.
The reason, as the blessed man came to understand from what he saw, was that the young man was unworthy. For it happened that he was not clean from defilement.
That blessed man also related another miracle like this one, concerning the power of holy Golgotha and the divine grace hidden within it.
Once, when a severe skin disease broke out on the face of blessed John the eunuch and was eating away at his whole face, both of them were distressed.
They suffered greatly over this, and blessed John hid himself, unwilling even to be seen by people. When their sorrow grew intense
and was consuming their hearts, the faithful Peter came to himself and burned with the Spirit and with divine fervor.
He took blessed John with him at night, and the two of them went to the holy Church of the Resurrection. When they went up to the site of holy Golgotha from the northern side,
since the place was quiet and secluded, they knelt down, pleading with our Lord with bitter tears and sighs.
When they had finished praying, they stood up and approached to bow before the venerated rock of holy Golgotha. Blessed John saw
something like a hand come out from there, approach his forehead, and wipe his whole face.
When morning came, he was found to be entirely healed, with no discomfort or trace of that disease.
These things demonstrate the divine power of the holy cross and give full assurance to our hope.
I think it fitting likewise to append to this account another miracle that happened to blessed John himself on another occasion,
to demonstrate their love for one another, their faith in God, and their confidence before him.
Once blessed John fell so gravely ill that his recovery was considered hopeless.
Father Peter was deeply distressed and pleaded unceasingly with the Lord for his recovery. A voice came to him, saying, “Take courage.
Look, I am granting him recovery because of your petition, and I am adding another twelve years to his life.” And this indeed happened.
Then something remarkable happened: when he recovered and began to regain his strength, his body began shedding thick layers of skin, from his nails up to his neck.
Everyone was distressed, fearing that as the peeling spread it might disfigure his face as well. But when Father Peter again pleaded and prayed earnestly, it spread no farther than his neck.
When he had recovered, his body and flesh became like those of a newborn child.
His voice, however, was so indistinct that he could not say anything clearly and intelligibly. When one of the recognized feast days arrived,
Father Peter, acting with divinely given assurance, urged him to celebrate the holy offering for them.
For both of them had been judged worthy of the honor of the priesthood, and blessed Peter of the episcopate as well.
Although he quite reasonably begged to be excused, since he could not speak and was unable to do it, Father Peter persisted in pleading with him and urging him,
saying, “There is no need for you to speak aloud. Just complete the prayers within your heart, for God hears even when we are silent.” Under this insistence, he agreed.
When he stood before the holy altar, he said clearly and intelligibly to the people, “Peace be with you all,” and in this way completed the entire holy offering.
Having received his former voice anew from God, as though he had never been ill, he continued afterward to speak well for all the rest of his life.
At this time, blessed John remained in a vision for three whole days.
He spoke to no one at all, but saw the awesome and glorious second coming of our Lord:
the heavens suddenly opening, the trumpets sounding, the tremors of the world, the transformation of the elements—that is, their alteration;
everything filled with light and terror, turmoil, trembling, and confusion; the angels running ahead;
and the foremost ranks of the heavenly powers: angels, archangels, authorities, dominions, glorious ones;
the ranks of the holy apostles, the prophets, the martyrs, and the righteous; the cherubim, the seraphim; and after them all, the adorable
and saving sign of our Lord’s cross, and the Lord himself, the Savior and Christ, coming in procession with the Father’s glory
and indescribable power; the thrones being prepared, and the divine and awesome court of judgment,
which was announced to us beforehand as a testimony, long ago and many times through the holy prophets and by the Judge and Savior himself.
He also saw a single altar standing on the earth, resembling in every respect the one still preserved among us even now, at which both of them used to minister.
Beside it stood a multitude of holy monks surrounding it, each holding his staff.
And suddenly there were the sounds of trumpets and the upheaval of the elements, and what looked like flying clouds,
carrying away from that altar the holy men standing beside it, to meet our Lord. When he had thus spent three days in such a vision
and had seen many other mysteries that a human being is not permitted to speak of, he afterward came to himself and remained stunned for about thirty days.
He did not wish to say anything to anyone—or rather, he was not even able to.
For in his mind he was entirely there, and no longer thought that he was living on earth. His face became like the face of an angel,
and his whole appearance was different from a human appearance. But this vision occurred much later, toward the end.
Since I have mentioned the altar, I will not conceal the sign that occurred at it when it was being consecrated, as blessed Peter himself often
told us. For when they later moved away during the Chalcedonian persecution and were living in Alexandria, they made this holy altar there.
While it was being consecrated, the blessed man himself clearly saw Saint Mark the Evangelist standing and consecrating it.
For this reason, grace accomplished such wonders and many mighty works and healings through his hands, which cannot be numbered.
We have neither the strength nor the time to recount them one by one.
But this vision, as I said, was revealed toward the end, while they were living in Alexandria and being persecuted for their orthodoxy.
But let us fulfill our promise and return to the point where we left our narrative,
explaining the reason that brought them to the monastery between Gaza and Maiuma, where, while living there, they were compelled to enter the priesthood.
Thus the holy city of Jerusalem received this rebuilding from Constantine, the Christian emperor.
At first it still had few inhabitants and no wall, since the former wall had been demolished by the Romans. There were very few houses and inhabitants in it.
Now the chief priests and bishops who subsequently held office in Jerusalem wanted many inhabitants to settle in the city
and many buildings to be built. They therefore gave permission to anyone who wished and was able to take, in any part of the city, whatever site
pleased him, free of charge and without payment, and build a dwelling there. Then the blessed Peter too, up near holy Zion,
at what is called the Tower of David [?], chose a site for himself and built a monastery there. It is still called the Monastery of the Iberians to this day.
It lies on the left as one approaches holy Zion from the tower's second gate.
He lived there in solitude with John, his companion in the solitary life. I will not pass over the miraculous sign that occurred there while they were building the place.
It was this: a certain well-known member of the clergy was their neighbor. He too had obtained a site and was putting up a building there.
When a dispute arose over the boundary, as happens between neighbors, John the eunuch was outside with the workers
and was appealing to the man gently and humbly. Such was his customary manner, for he imitated the humility of Moses.
But the man who was acting unjustly, as though he had suffered some terrible injury merely because John had spoken against him at all, struck the blessed man violently on the cheek,
imitating the servant of Caiaphas. After receiving the blow and suffering great pain, John made no reply at all.
Instead, he left the workers and the man, who was full of anger, and went inside to Father Peter, holding his cheek in his hand and groaning.
The blow was painful. But the two of them knelt down and gave thanks to our Lord,
who had considered them worthy to share in his blows. Without saying anything to that man, and after the builders had come in from
their work, they prepared to move away and leave that place. By the following morning, that wretched man was dead and buried, although previously there had been nothing wrong with him.
Thus all the inhabitants of Jerusalem would know that, because of the insult inflicted on these holy men, God the Judge had not withheld his anger—
he who always helped them. So the two of them continued alone in that place,
and they still had some money left from what they had managed to take with them when they departed.
They had already distributed much of it everywhere to holy monks and to the poor. They decided to make a good investment with what remained
by welcoming and providing rest for strangers and poor people who came from everywhere to worship at the holy places.
So they laid in ample supplies, and these strangers and sojourners welcomed strangers as Abraham had done.
Although they were entirely inexperienced in such services, it often happened that they had as many as ten tables in a single day,
especially on the major feast days. Even with so many guests, they served them entirely by themselves, going out themselves [?].
For cheerfulness of soul and the love of Christ overcame the weakness of their nature. By that love they were strengthened, and they were comforted by miracles.
And so, once, when a crowd of guests gathered around them, they ran short of provisions. Since the circumstances were pressing, they were distressed.
They cried out secretly to God in their hearts, ashamed of the hardship the guests were suffering.
But when they entered the storeroom to investigate whether some remaining supplies might have been overlooked and left behind,
all the containers were found full, each containing the kind of provision it had held before.
After they had spent a long time receiving guests in this way, the holy Zeno, the monk and prophet, finally advised them—
he was a disciple of the great Silvanus, who was renowned everywhere—
to enter a monastery again and receive further training through submission and humility. He said to them:
“Now that you have practiced hospitality, come, henceforth practice the monastic life, receiving training in the monastery.
For this is more beneficial to those who are still young in years.”
So they entered one of the holy monasteries and conducted themselves with complete obedience, submission, and abstinence.
Consequently, the devil, unable to bear the rigor of their asceticism, set about bringing them down from their way of asceticism and cheerfulness,
devising various temptations for them. Indeed, on one occasion,
while Abba Peter was standing in the choir and chanting with the brothers, he made a naked and very beautiful woman appear before him.
But Peter, who alone saw the apparition and considered even the sight of it a defilement, covered his face, turning this way and that.
While the brothers were astonished and puzzled about what the cause could be, he cried out loudly, saying:
“Our Lord Jesus, remove from before my eyes this ugly and filthy image
and the loathsomeness of this apparition, and leave me alone!” When the evil one heard the name of our Savior, he immediately became invisible.
After they had spent some time in the monastery, as the holy Zeno had advised, they returned again, with his knowledge,
to their own monastery. They lived in solitude in the Holy City, no longer receiving guests in the same way.
For that money had run out, having been well spent. They wore themselves out with great asceticism and harsh disciplines.
But they were not allowed to remain there for very long. The empress Eudocia, who was the wife of the faithful emperor Theodosius the Younger,
emulating the zeal of Melania, whom we mentioned earlier, also longed for solitude and residence in the Holy City,
so that she might be near enough to pay homage in person to the saving sufferings endured for us by Christ, the King of glory.
Traveling with imperial pomp, she made her journey through all the cities and came to the Holy City for which she had longed, and was granted the honor of worshiping there.
When she learned that Abba Peter was living there, she eagerly sought to see him, as the woman who had raised him and had been a mother to him with loving affection in the palace.
At first, however, he pleaded to be allowed not to leave his cell, because he considered it a temptation.
But when she persisted, saying that if he was unwilling to come to her, she would certainly come to him,
since she was preparing to travel from there to holy Zion, he feared the honors and people’s envy, and came out once and spoke with her.
When she had been edified by his great gentleness, humility, chastity, and wisdom as well, he heard her say, “Blessed are you, my son, because the good
is what you have chosen for yourself. Remember me in your holy prayers.” But he answered her, “What confidence does a sinner have to pray?”
She said to him, “Let your sins be on my head, my son.” And so he returned to his cell and remained in solitude.
But when she again persisted in her desire to come to him, he immediately hurried to the holy prophet Zeno mentioned earlier.
As was his custom, he revealed his thoughts to him, for he always discussed them with him. He heard him say, “Save, save your soul!”
So, persuaded by his advice, he left Jerusalem, the holy city, and left his monastery to some men who had also renounced the world,
and came to live in a monastic community situated between Gaza and the small town called Maiuma.
At that time it was full of many holy men, monks who bore their crosses.
The arrangement of his move to that place was the work of divine providence.
For God, who is wise in everything and cares for our souls, had prepared beforehand for that city on the seashore, so deeply Christian,
a high priest and bishop worthy of it, especially at a time of chastisement, when such a man was needed:
a champion of devotion to God, both a preacher and a guardian of the orthodox faith,
and an ambassador on behalf of our souls, possessing great confidence before our Lord, to make atonement for the sins of the people, as it is written,
and able to sympathize with our weakness by continually pleading on our behalf. So, while
he was living in this monastic community, he would constantly go with John, his cell companion, to holy Zeno, who at that time was living in the village of Kefar Searta,
fifteen miles from Gaza. He discussed all his thoughts with him and pursued the path of godly virtue with still greater fervor.
He was greatly loved by him and received a share of his grace. This blessed man used to relate:
“Once, when I came to him, holy Zeno had stood up to pray. Turning toward me, he said to me, ‘Pray.’
“When I remained silent, he turned again and said to me, ‘Pray.’ He did this three times in the same way.
“Astonished and exasperated with him, I said to him, ‘Forgive me, my lord, father. Do you not know that I am a layman and a sinner?’ And he said,
“‘Yes, yes. Forgive me.’ Then he offered a prayer and sat down.” Seven days later his ordination took place. And in what way?
For we should not pass over this in silence either. While he was still living in the holy city, Juvenal repeatedly tried,
who was its bishop at the time, to ordain him, but he could not,
because God was hiding him. All this happened while an assembly was being held in holy Zion.
Juvenal tried to send some determined men to seize him from his cell, which was nearby.
As they were about to come, an angel appeared to him and said, “Look, they are coming to take you for ordination. But get up and flee from here.”
After escaping in this way, he guarded himself even more carefully. Now, while he was living in the region of Maiuma, the bishop
of that place at the time was Paul, Juvenal’s nephew.
He sent word to him that, at the beginning of his residence there, Paul himself had given his word to the blessed Peter, who had asked him not to lay hands on him.
When many bishops gathered for a synod at the commemoration of Victor, the gloriously victorious martyr, he revealed the secret to one of them and urged him to perform the ordination.
He took as his helper the blessed Irenion, the abbot of that monastery, who was a companion, neighbor, and confidant of these holy men.
With his help, he suddenly took them by surprise and ordained them both priests, using much force and coercion.
Then Peter remembered and understood the foreknowledge and prophecy of Saint Zeno.
Yet, although he had received the laying on of hands in this way, he remained for seven years unwilling to take part in the priestly ministry,
until he was also deemed worthy of the honor of being a bishop, at the time of the rebellion and transgression at Chalcedon.
For when the written denial of all these rebellious bishops and the confirmation of Leo’s wicked Tome were reported everywhere,
along with the revival of the perverse teachings of Nestorius, Dioscorus, the archbishop of Egypt
and champion of the truth, who fought for the fear of God, was sent into exile
because he refused to consent to wickedness. Theodoret and Ibas, however, who were among these men and who had already
been deposed and anathematized because of his obvious wickedness, were received without a trial.
And Flavian, who had been bishop of Constantinople and had been deposed for this same reason, after
his death they reinstated him. And Juvenal, the so-called high priest of Jerusalem,
having consented to lawlessness and lent a hand in it, and having preferred the lot of Judas the betrayer, returned with great pomp.
Yet before going up to the synod, he had rejected the so-called Tome of Leo
and mocked the wickedness in it. He had testified to all the clergy and monks in Palestine, saying,
“The doctrine it contains is Jewish and belongs to Simon the Magician, and anyone who agrees with it ought to be circumcised.”
When these things became known to the clergy and the holy monks in Palestine, they were stirred by divine zeal.
First they went out onto the road to meet Juvenal. They earnestly begged him to remember his words, reject wickedness, and fight for the truth.
When he would not be persuaded, they gathered together in the holy city, having in their midst our Lord Jesus Christ, who had been denied by the wicked.
But he supports his truth and his orthodox church, which he redeemed with his blood.
They were inspired by his grace, and with them were zealous orthodox bishops and the holy Romanus, the father of the monks.
They chose the blessed Theodosius from the holy order, a man who had practiced the monastic way of life from his youth,
adorned with all the gifts of the fear of the Lord, who had already demonstrated many struggles on behalf of the orthodox faith, including at that wicked council itself.
They appointed him chief priest and shepherd of the holy city of Jerusalem. Having received the priesthood from God, with complete diligence he exercised care
and took pains to ensure that the apostolic faith was preserved pure in the churches under him.
He therefore chose from the order of the holy, cross-bearing monks holy men who were especially well attested in every aspect of evangelical conduct and blameless faith.
He ordained these men as bishops and martyrs, and sent to each city the man suited to it.
The people of each city themselves issued a decree for the man chosen from among them. Thus they were received with complete joy and gladness.
For when he performed ordinations, the patriarch himself testified in a loud voice to those being ordained, saying:
“I ordain you as martyrs and heralds of the orthodox faith, for the present time needs bishops like these.”
Then the inhabitants of Maiuma near Gaza, stirred by divine power and knowing the blessed Peter from the long time he had lived among them,
displaying every kind of virtue, immediately all rushed to the place where he was living in solitude and seized him.
He struggled hard against them and shut and bolted the doors when he saw that they had come upon him like a band of raiders.
Nevertheless, with great force and love, the people took him, carried him away, and put him in a litter.
And a large number of prominent leaders, the clergy themselves, and a great crowd of people [?] accompanied them.
They brought him to the holy city so that there, through the chief priests, they might be granted him as their own shepherd and bishop.
As they were traveling along the road, when evening was already approaching, they came to a village called Suca.
They lodged in the inns beside it, but they arranged for the holy man to lodge in a certain upper room in the village, together with men capable of guarding him.
When midnight came, he was distressed by his thoughts and his heart was troubled, because he always fled from honor, as I said earlier.
He considered himself unworthy of the honor of the priesthood and resolved that, if necessary, he would rather die than accept such a burden.
And since it was an untimely hour, and they were all exhausted by the toil of the journey and overcome by sleep,
He asked those guarding him to let him go out onto the roof in front of the upper room, as though to attend to a bodily need.
When they gave him permission and he went out alone, he ran to throw himself down from the height onto the rocks below,
expecting one of two things to happen: either he would somehow escape, or, being crippled and no longer useful,
he would be released from the coercion of those taking him along. But just as he was about to do this, a voice came to him, saying,
“Peter, Peter, if you do this, you have no share with me.” And so, restrained from his attempt, he was taken to Jerusalem.
There he caused much disturbance, accusing himself and loudly proclaiming many charges,
through which he thought he could show himself unworthy of the priesthood, and he testified to them before the man who was to ordain him.

Nevertheless, when he received the decree and ordination from divine grace itself, he was unwilling to minister even then. Although he had been bound to a priestly position, he did not at first accept
the ministry, though everyone, including the patriarch himself, urged and implored him, until once again the divine voice itself threatened him and gave him a command.
And so, while the service was being celebrated in the holy church of the place called Siloam, he, of his own accord, to everyone's amazement and astonishment,
came running out. They gathered with the archbishop and the other bishops, all of them coming out to meet him
with joy, gladness, and wonder, praising God. They had been gripped by great distress and anxiety,
lest his refusal become a cause of stumbling for many. But when he came to the holy church of Maiuma,
honored in procession by them all, he took his seat [?] on the throne on the seventh of the month of August. It was a great, holy, heavenly festival, bringing life to the souls of them all.
While the people pressed eagerly forward, and everyone longed to receive the saving mysteries from his holy hands,
he again hesitated, out of great modesty, to make the offering himself. Instead, he implored the bishops and clergy to perform the holy services.
At first he was unwilling to stand before the holy altar and celebrate the holy Eucharist, until the people grew weary and agitated and convinced him that they truly believed
he was planning to flee. They rushed forward, threatening to burn him and the church unless he celebrated the service for them.
And so, under compulsion, he stood before the holy altar. Let whoever transcribes copy what follows.
But let the greatness of God's visitation, his love for humanity, and his power be openly proclaimed and made known
everywhere, to reassure and strengthen the faithful and to establish the orthodox faith.
For we cannot keep silent about what we heard and were assured of through the blessed man's own testimony and through many who were then close to him and served as priests alongside him.
For, since he could not yet recite the holy prayers well and had not practiced beforehand, he was suddenly compelled to stand before the altar
and perform the holy service, with great fear, alarm, and trembling. Some of the clergy stood beside him,
so that they could remind him if he omitted anything required. When the time came and he made the invocation of the Holy Spirit,
And he completed the whole Eucharist. When he came to the awesome breaking of the bread, he did so with much sobbing, heartfelt contrition, and many tears.
As he broke it according to his custom, all of it spurted blood, so that the entire holy table was sprinkled.
Astonished and pale with trembling, he drew back and no longer dared approach to break the remaining loaves.
In his agitation he turned and saw the Lord standing beside him, encouraging him and saying to him:
“Bishop, break it; do not be afraid. I have done this for my glory, not for yours,
so that everyone may learn where the truth is and who those are who hold the orthodox faith.”
That miracle which happened then is still recounted by everyone to this day. He remained in his holy church
for about six months, while everyone celebrated and rejoiced and pronounced the inhabitants of the city of Maiuma blessed
because of God's favor and his provision of such a bishop. They held him as an angel and clung to him with affection and love.
The devil, who fights against God and is envious, that first apostate and the counselor and supporter of apostates,
could not bear to see all this glory of God and the salvation of human beings. Fearing that there might be a reversal
of the policy established in writing at Chalcedon against the fear of God—and since his commands were readily obeyed—he brought it about through an imperial decree
that the holy and true bishops, zealous for the fear of God, who had been ordained by the great and apostolic bishop Theodosius
