in all the cities of Palestine, should be driven from their sees. If they were unwilling, they were to be expelled by force and subjected to punishment.
But Theodosius himself, the chief shepherd, wherever he might be found, was to suffer the death penalty, for the man he called emperor had issued an edict against him.
At that time they all escaped and withdrew, for the patriarch Theodosius himself had advised this. Judging what was pleasing to God, he told them
that the heralds of the truth should be preserved, so that, through their death and murder, the orthodox peoples would not be deprived of those who built them up and sustained
them. Then the blessed Peter withdrew to Egypt and, by God's will, came to the city of Alexandria.
He remained hidden there in the days of that rebel Proterius, and he was a support and consolation to all the orthodox.
While none of those who held to the truth dared appear in public, neither cleric nor monk, he remained in hiding
and celebrated the divine services. He gave the provisions of life to all who sought them, and did not allow them to lose heart
or to diminish in zeal and faith. He was also deemed worthy to see the following awesome vision.
While a spectacle for all the people was being held in the city, in the place called the theater, the faithful people were burning with zeal.
Suddenly, moved by divine power, they began to cry out: “Dioscorus to the city! The orthodox bishop to the city!
The confessor to his throne! Let the bones of Proterius be burned! Banish Judas into exile! Throw Judas out!”
And as they shouted countless other acclamations, they asked that Dioscorus, the champion of reverence for God, should return from his unjust exile
and take his throne, but that the ravenous wolf who fought against God, the new Caiaphas, should be cast out and completely expelled from the holy churches.
But those officials, eager to please the man then in power in everything and devising schemes for their own advantage,
brought a large force of armed soldiers and surrounded the theater. Threatening slaughter and murder, they terrified this entire crowd,
so that, as they fled outside and trampled one another in the theater’s narrow entrances, many died.
At that time, then, the blessed Peter, who was in hiding, as I have said, was celebrating the holy mysteries.
And when he fell into a trance, he saw many souls being escorted by angels and carried up to heaven.
When some people came from the city and reported what had happened, it was found that the number
of those who had died violently in that trampling and confusion was the same as the number of souls the blessed man had counted while experiencing that vision.
And like that robber who is pronounced blessed, these people too, at that very moment, gained the very same crown in a single hour through their confession of faith.
For such a reward is reserved for those who struggle and earnestly contend for the orthodox faith,
even if they show their zeal only at the end of their lives. But when the blessed Peter could no longer remain hidden from the wicked Proterius,
who pursued him to harm him even to the point of death and sent murderers by night to seize and kill him,
he was able to escape, because our Lord, who rescued and sheltered him, revealed to him the hidden plot.
For when those who had been sent approached the door of the place inside the city where he was hiding and knocked,
pretending to be acquaintances belonging to the orthodox believers, they pleaded that a little child who was in danger
should be baptized before he died. But a holy voice told him, “Do not open; they are plotting against you.”
Then he said to the brothers who were with him, “Let no one open the door. Instead, do whatever you see me doing.”
After they quickly knelt and stood up, he and the brothers with him cried out loudly, “Our Father in heaven!
Look, robbers! Help!” When the neighbors and those nearby heard and came running, the plotters fled.
And so, having been rescued from the hunters’ snares, as it is written, they left that place and moved to the upper regions of the Thebaid.
When he came to the city of Oxyrhynchus, [?] named Moses, a man who loved Christ and the saints and was endowed with virtues in faith and willingness.
The blessed man used to relate concerning him that, although he had an annual income of two thousand denarii, he distributed half of it to the saints, the poor, and strangers.
The other half was for his own essential needs and for the taxes owed to the public treasury.
Now this Oxyrhynchus is a large and prosperous city of the Thebaid, in which the grace of Christ reigned so completely that, when they all became
Christians—no fewer than ten thousand—a gathering of monks who lived in the monasteries around it.
While he was there, it happened at that time that the wicked Proterius, who fought against God, drew up and composed a written anathema, supposedly, to lead the simple astray,
and in it made deceitful and concealed reference to the wickedness of the Council of Chalcedon, with great malicious cunning and shamelessness,
mixing poison with honey. But when this was read before all the people, and he was unable to shake any of those who were firmly established,
he sent a copy of it to the bishops under him, those who had agreed to submit to his rebellion,
ordering it to be read before all the people of every city. When the bishop of Oxyrhynchus received it,
and read it before all the people, with the devil also helping him, he brazenly sought to mislead and unsettle many of the orthodox.
While many were in danger of stumbling, since they were simple and unpracticed in such cunning and pretense,
the blessed Peter was urged by the leaders of the city, and by the very man who had received him, who was zealous,
and by the holy monks, to read it, expose the deceit and the scheme, and proclaim the truth openly before all the people.
He begged off at length, since he was unaccustomed to disturbances of this kind and to speaking openly before the people. Nevertheless, when pressed, he committed himself
to bearing witness. So they took him and stationed him in the public square, at an elevated spot on the base of a column on which stood a statue of the emperor.
Holding that treacherous document in his hands, he pondered and struggled
over how to expose the ambush hidden in it. Suddenly he saw the blessed Theodosius, bishop of Jerusalem,
that new James, who had ordained him and who had already met his end through confession and martyrdom in the imperial city,
in the days of the God-hating Emperor Marcian. We will recount the manner of his death later, if God permits.
He saw him standing at his right, pointing with his finger, showing and exposing the wickedness concealed in every statement.
Whatever he heard from him, he spoke to the people, while our Lord stood nearby and helped him, granting him both boldness and grace.
Having thus persuaded the people and strengthened them all, he snatched them from the snares of error, while everyone regarded and praised him as an angel,
putting to shame the repulsive dragon, his servants, and those who gratified him. At that time,
the blessed Dioscorus, the archbishop, having fought the good fight of confession and completed his race,
and having kept the apostolic faith without transgression to the end, died in exile in the city of Gangra, the metropolis of Paphlagonia,
after serving as bishop for seven years and three months. The day on which he died was the seventh of September.
When the bitter and painful news about him was announced to the cities of Alexandria, the congregations of the orthodox people,
and the holy monks and nuns, were broken in spirit by intense sorrow and distress, having now given up hope of their deliverance.
But that savage, blood-drinking wolf, Proterius, was exulting and beside himself with great joy and delight,
as though his rule were now secure and free from disturbance.
From then on, he inflicted terrible evils on the laypeople and monks who were unwilling to enter into communion with him,
bribing the officials and, through them, bringing every kind of humiliation and unbearable distress upon the orthodox.
He brought bands of savage, barbarous soldiers into the city, and committed unspeakable evils, full of countless causes for lamentation,
and mercilessly performed acts contrary to the laws of nature, until he even extended his madness to the holy virgins.
But that righteous, mighty, and patient Judge was not going to tolerate such evils any longer—he who strikes and heals, chastises and restores to health.
Instead, the Lord awoke as though from sleep and made his spear flash, and with it killed the twisting dragon—I mean Marcian, the new Assyrian—
when an angel struck him on the neck, as though with a sword, inflicting an incurable wound, as those who saw it with their own eyes and verified it testified. Then,
the blessed Peter left Oxyrhynchus and returned to Alexandria. It was God who brought him back there,
because of the divine arrangement that was to take place, to comfort the faithful people and to restore and establish the orthodox faith.
It happened in this way. When news of Marcian’s death reached the city of Alexandria—
the man who had been the leader, cause, and supporter of such evils—the faithful people, who had already been losing strength and suffering distress
because of the many afflictions and persecutions that had come upon them, as has been said, and whose hands had grown weak, found a time of relief and came to life again.
They offered praise, thanksgiving, and glory to Christ our Savior, who had not utterly abandoned them in anger into the hands of that destructive, blood-drinking wolf.
Seeing that the time was favorable and welcome to them, communities of holy monks gathered—not only those within the city itself,
but also those nearby, in the place called the Enaton, in the Octodecaton and the Eikoston, and in the other holy monasteries—
together with all the faithful and zealous people of the city of Alexandria. They had as their leader and foremost man, who also

stirred them up and encouraged them in this according to God’s will, the blessed ascetic and great prophet Longinus, the father of the monks. After they had all deliberated together, he sent men suited to the task.
They seized from the desert, without his having learned of it beforehand or having any inkling at all, the holy Timothy, that renowned confessor and true witness,
who had already been honored with the priesthood by the great Cyril, the archbishop, together with Anatolius, his steadfast brother, who equaled him in zeal.
He was a man adorned with every kind of apostolic conduct and grace, and especially with steadfastness and fervent zeal for the orthodox faith.
When they brought him into the city, to the church called the Caesareum, and the whole city, so to speak, had gathered as one, including women and children,
together with the holy monks, they eagerly sought to ordain him and appoint him chief priest, a herald and champion of reverence for God.
But only one of the orthodox bishops was found there: Eusebius of Pelusium.
Because these others were being persecuted and were hiding, and did not dare to appear in public, when it became known to the people, by God's will,
that our blessed Peter was there in hiding, the people hurried over and suddenly came to the place where the blessed man was staying.
They seized him by force, carried him on their shoulders, and brought him to the Caesareum, where the crowds of people were gathered,
as the ancient laws and customs allowed them to do in times of persecution.
The blessed man had already been fully assured by God that this was his will, just as he had often revealed it secretly to his beloved friends,
and likewise to Bishop Timothy, while God's grace was then close at hand and bringing everything about.
But while everyone was distracted by joy and delight at such a prospect, blessed Peter managed to go unnoticed, passing through the crowd and going away to hide.
The Lord concealed him—the Lord who had revealed this to him when he was afraid to do such a thing—just as with Philip the apostle, who, after baptizing Candace's eunuch,
immediately disappeared from sight. For the blessed man always fled from human honor and praise,
regarding it as a disturbance of the undistracted solitude he loved and of his untroubled communion with God,
although he was not allowed to carry his purpose through to the end as he desired. For when the ordination of the great high priest Timothy had thus
taken place by God's decree and good pleasure, through the election, efforts, and formal vote of the people of Alexandria
and of the holy, cross-bearing monks, and inexpressible joy and exultation filled everyone's soul,
while the people were celebrating and rejoicing, that wicked and utterly impure Proterius saw that he was in danger and became still more savage.
He bribed the officials with a great deal of gold, especially the man called the military commander, whose name was Dionysius, a murderous man of violent temper,
and stirred him to such madness that he rushed upon God's holy church with a large force of armed soldiers, savage and barbarous,
to kill many laypeople, monks, and nuns without mercy, and to cut down many others with blows and leave them half dead.
Finally, he did not shrink from assaulting the divine baptistery and, from the holy Jordan itself—that is, from the very basin of the revered baptismal font—
seizing Saint Timothy like a bandit, together with his brother Anatolius, and having him taken to Taposiris, a fortress in the desert thirty miles from the city.
They imprisoned him there under military guard, so that henceforth, when that wicked Proterius found an opportunity suited to his madness,
he could again inflict many evils upon the monks and laypeople who were unwilling to share in his wickedness, especially upon
those who had worked for the ordination of blessed Timothy. When the people could no longer endure these things, and had lost hope, and their souls were now filled and sated with distress,
they blazed with the zeal of martyrs, drew up for battle against the soldiers every day, and started a civil war, with killings and bloodshed.
Then the city officials and the man called the military commander became afraid that so great a city belonging to the emperor might be destroyed,

since he had not yet learned of these events, nor had they informed him of them, and he might become angry with them. For news of the accession and proclamation of the new emperor Leo had already spread everywhere.
They agreed together to take Proterius too outside the city, bring him to some place, and keep him under guard,
until they could inform the emperor and he could issue whatever order he thought best concerning each of them. So when Proterius was being taken out by the soldiers,
one of them became inflamed with zeal and killed him, on the fourth of Nisan, twenty days after the ordination of the blessed Timothy.
He had occupied the throne for five years and six months. When this happened, everyone fled together, laypeople and soldiers alike.
He was left lying in the street like a pig or a dog—creatures he had resembled in his conduct and his wantonness—having brought destruction upon himself.
As for the things that happened amid these events, which are beyond anything the ears
of God-fearing people can bear, we leave them to others to recount and write down.
For although he deserved what he suffered, it is not fitting for us either to hear such things or to recount them.
Yet, as it is written, we see that the divine word was fulfilled in him: “Evil will hunt down the unjust man to destroy him,”
and, “You have brought the proud low like the slain,” and, “The Lord fights against the proud,” and, “The wicked man is kept for the day of his slaughter.”
When these things were reported to Emperor Leo, he was moved with compassion for the troubles that had afflicted the city of Alexandria throughout this whole period.
Taking pity on those who remained, he ordered that the blessed Timothy, who had received ordination from God, should enter and take possession of his throne,
so that the city might be at peace, the people might find relief, and they might receive consolation for the evils that had passed. This indeed came to them through the return of the blessed Timothy.
For everywhere one could see the joy, gladness, and rejoicing that filled the city, while great crowds of unbelievers hurried to receive baptism.
To put it briefly, the city of Alexandria was heaven in those days. Now, after the blessed Timothy had remained in the episcopate for seven years,
the envious demon, unable to bear seeing the salvation of humanity, once again stirred up the bishops in anger to evil zeal and envy—
the bishops everywhere, and especially the bishop of Constantinople and the bishop of Rome.
For the blessed man's standing, reputation, conduct, and boldness were a source of shame and reproach to them,
since every day the wicked Council of Chalcedon was publicly anathematized by him and by the bishops under him, as well as by clergy, monks, and laypeople.
And after they had employed intense efforts in every direction, gifts, and the patronage of wicked men—
when he found that those who held power at that time were overcome by the love of money—they did not cease their intrigues and wickedness
until, amid the killing of many of the people and the shedding of blood, they brought about the banishment of the blessed Timothy
to the city of Gangra, where the crown of confession had been completed for the victorious archbishop Dioscorus, his fellow confessor.
This was the reason why the blessed Peter could not withdraw from human society, as he prayed and longed to do,
and enjoy the solitude he loved. For when Timothy, the archbishop, departed and was handed over to exile by imperial command and authority,
Another of the priests succeeded him by imperial command; his name was Timothy.
He was also called by the nickname Salophakros, and he likewise held to the false doctrine of the Chalcedonians. When Peter, who pleased God and shared the zeal
of the great Moses, saw the distress of the faithful brothers, who had been left amid death and without those who would build them up and support them,
and were in danger of being shaken from the truth of the faith, he was seized with divine zeal and exerted himself to the point of death,
pondering and meditating on these universally known words of the apostle: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?”
Leaving the solitude he loved, since this was no time for it, he went again to the city of Alexandria and the holy monasteries around it,
and to many other cities and villages of Egypt, traveling everywhere in secret.
He built up and strengthened the congregations of the orthodox and, like another Paul the apostle, became all things to everyone.
Through his conduct and manner, in word and deed, he provided an example for teaching godly living and divine zeal.
As for the great wonders and signs he performed there through divine grace and the power that accompanied him, and the many healings and mighty deeds,
it is beyond our weakness to write them all down. We will recall one or two, but leave the rest to those
who learned of them through experience and by seeing them for themselves, to recount and relate. The daughter of one of the city's prominent men was suffering from a severe illness.
She was his only daughter, and he loved her as an only daughter is loved. This girl's mother was a woman who loved Christ
and was a believer, and she took great delight in the holy ones. Her father, though a Christian, was deeply attached to error and to friendship with pagan philosophers.
For this reason, when he received assurances from a man who was a leader of the sorcerers that he would heal the girl if they took her and brought her by night to the Serapeum,
where he would perform upon her the rites and defilements of the magical arts, he readily agreed and was prepared to hand the girl over.
When her mother learned this from a servant who had discovered it, a Christian and a very faithful man, she immediately sent word to the blessed Peter, informing him of the devil's plan.
She begged him not to neglect her, her husband, and the girl, who were in danger of falling into true death by provoking the Lord.
When the blessed man heard this, he was inflamed with zeal and cried out in a loud voice, “Lord, may that wicked man not live!”
Having said this, he immediately took some of the holy men who were with him, and that night they went to the girl's mother.
He found her sitting beside her daughter, racked with weeping and lamentation, while also keeping watch so that her husband would not hand the girl over to that wicked man.
He ordered everyone whose presence was unnecessary to go outside, then took oil and anointed the girl.
After giving her the holy mysteries, comforting her mother with many words of consolation, and encouraging her to put her trust without any doubt in Christ, the Lord of life,
he returned to where he was staying. The following day, the girl was suddenly found to be well
and free from that severe illness. But that philosopher who fought against God was buried dead.
The sentence pronounced by that saint was thus swiftly carried out. In his indignation he had cried out, saying, “Lord, may that wicked man not live!”
This was so that the miracle would become known throughout the city, and everyone would glorify God for his grace bestowed on his saints,
and would run to the blessed man and attach themselves to him, and be strengthened still further in the orthodox faith.
For this sign also happened at that time. He was going by night with his companions to the house of a rich man to visit someone who was sick,
and was passing a place where a very large statue of Julian the Apostate stood. A demon produced the following apparition:
the statue came down from its pedestal and ran after them. When those walking with him became aware of the clatter and commotion,
and saw the apparition, they were bewildered and cried out, calling on the blessed man to help them.
But he appeared not to have noticed, although he knew very well. He continued on his way without turning around.
But when they were frightened and clung to his clothes, the blessed man turned around, invoked the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and blew upon the apparition.
Immediately it dissolved like smoke and vanished from sight. The blessed man also used to relate this incident, which happened in Alexandria in those days:
A certain devout man urged some of the holy men to come to his house, bless it, and share a meal with him.
The Alexandrians are very attentive to this practice and willingly take trouble over it.
The man was distinguished and well known. He also urged them to take me along with them.
Those fathers knew that my poor self found invitations of this kind difficult because of my great weakness.
Nevertheless, they persisted and pressed me strongly, saying, “Since the man is zealous and attentive, we ought not to give him cause to stumble.”
When we arrived, we reclined at the table. While we were eating, he began giving orders to the slaves who were serving,
and rebuking them with improper words belonging to the world's evil habits, as though he had forgotten with whom he was reclining and eating.
While he persisted in using these words, a voice came to me, saying, “Peter, Peter! My name is being blasphemed, and you sit there at your ease!”
No one heard the voice, he said, except me alone. Alarmed and weeping, I waited to be completely certain.
When the voice had come three times, I could no longer hold back my tears. I withdrew from among the others,
as though I urgently needed to relieve myself. In this way I went out and ran to my cell, sighing all along the way
and mourning. I reflected on how nothing escapes the eye that never sleeps—not even things that seem insignificant, neither a deed nor a word.
This, then, is what the wise Solomon said: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole inhabited world,
and he who holds all things has knowledge of the voice. Therefore no one who speaks unrighteousness remains hidden,
nor does he escape the judgment that brings reproof. The report of his words comes before the Lord for the rebuke of his wicked deeds.”
For the ear of jealousy hears everything. And our Lord himself said in the Gospel that we will give an account on the day of judgment for an idle word.
Yet that blessed man used to say that this became a means of salvation and a change for the better for the one who read them.
For the Lord does not desire the sinner’s death, but rather that he should turn back and live.
We must not omit this frightening and terrifying story either, which that blessed man also related as having happened at that time.
“For when I was about to offer the Eucharist,” he said, “outside the city, in one of the holy monasteries, some friends arrived before the consecration.
They were talking about something that had happened in the city, which offered neither edification nor benefit to those listening.
I remained silent, not accepting what was being said,
but neither did I stop them, so as not to embarrass them, for they were among the distinguished men of the city.
Instead, I passed over these things in silence and went in to offer the Eucharist. When I stood before the holy altar,
I saw an angel, frightening and terrifying in appearance, who came in anger, seized me around the waist, and wanted to throw me down through a window.
As I wept and wailed and asked what the reason was, he said,
‘Why, when you were about to enter into God’s service and stand before the holy altar, did you let yourself be drawn into talk like this?’
When I said, ‘You know, Lord, that I did not assent to it even by a gesture, and that none of what was said entered my heart at all,’ he said,
‘But why did you let yourself listen to such idle talk at all?’
None of those nearby heard these things or saw the appearance of that angel; only I did.
They could only see that I was trembling and gasping, and mourning in distress. Finally, the angel said,
‘Look, you have been forgiven this one time. From now on, take care, when you are about to stand before the altar and celebrate the mysteries, to stand serene and pure,
guarding yourself against every distraction and idle talk.’ When the angel had said this, he disappeared.”
That blessed man carefully observed this until his last breath. Now all these things, and others like them and still greater, when
they became known to the fathers in Palestine, and to the brothers and the Orthodox people, stirred and inflamed them all
with love for their holy father and bishop. And many holy men from Palestine came to him,
because the flock was rightfully his, and he should not neglect it, since all this time it had been bereft of his leadership and spiritual teaching.
So, after spending a considerable time in Alexandria and the rest of Egypt, and amply building them up and strengthening them, he was finally persuaded, as I have said—
or rather, he was also commanded by God, without whom he did nothing—and returned to the regions of Palestine.
When he came to the city of Ascalon and was joyfully received by the fathers and brothers there, he stayed in a village called Palaea, ten stadia from the city.
While he was living there, many people came to him from everywhere. Some of them he strengthened.
Others he enlightened and added to the orthodox church. Still others he trained to renounce the vanity of the world completely,
urging them to pursue perfection, distribute their possessions to the poor, take up the cross of Christ, and follow him alone.
Among these were also the blessed Procopius, who was chaste in every respect and whom he truly fashioned into a man of God, and Cyril, that lamb
of Christ. He brought both of them out of the world and led them to the dwelling place of angels. And Theodore, who was a lawyer,
who later also became heir to his gospel way of life, his zeal, and the leadership of his monastery, together with Abba John, the venerable elder,
who was loved and cherished and was adorned with every monastic virtue, especially humility.
He also drew many others, not only men but women too, to the service of Christ, urging them to take up the gentle yoke of virginity.
